Markup in text: **bold**, *italic*, and [[words|colour]] to tie words to a figure colour (parcel = orange rising air, env = violet surrounding air, dew = teal dew point). The lessons tell no story: the radio talks and the locals asking forecast questions (by forecast "id") are in data/radio.
title: Vertical giants and rare boss clouds
teaches: How a cumulus grows into a thunderstorm, estimating lightning distance, and spotting rare mountain-wave and shear clouds

blocks.text: When a thermal rises, cools to its dew point, and begins condensing into a cumulus cloud, the latent heat released by condensation slows its cooling rate to about 5 °C per kilometre. As long as the surrounding atmosphere gets colder with height faster than 5 °C per kilometre, the cloudy air stays warmer and less dense than its neighbours and keeps surging upward. How tall a cumulus heap grows depends on where it finally loses that temperature lead.

Three factors control where the rising air stops. First, **sunlight** warming the ground sets the starting temperature of the thermals. Second, low-level **moisture** sets the height of the cloud base, determining how soon the rising parcel switches to the slower 5 °C per kilometre cooling rate. Third, a stable [[inversion|env]] aloft can cap the cloud completely, just as an inversion flattens stratocumulus on the low floor. When a rising cloud top pokes into a warmer layer of air above it, the cloudy parcel immediately becomes colder and denser than its surroundings and cannot climb any higher.

Meteorologists classify cumulus clouds into three species according to their vertical growth. **Cumulus humilis** is small and flattened, wider than it is tall, and signals fair weather. **Cumulus mediocris** grows roughly as tall as it is wide. **Cumulus congestus** builds into tall, billowing cauliflower towers, and it is the stage to watch closely: on a deeply unstable day, a congestus tower can keep growing into a full thunderstorm.

Forecasters and glider pilots track this vertical growth on a temperature-height chart called a **sounding**. Twice a day, weather stations release balloons carrying a radio transmitter, thermometer, and humidity sensor that measure the temperature and dew point every few seconds as the balloon ascends.

In the figure below, the solid violet line shows the balloon’s report of the surrounding air temperature at each altitude. (The dashed violet line shows the cooler dawn profile before sunlight warmed the ground.) The teal line shows the dew point, and the orange line traces a rising parcel, cooling at 10 °C per kilometre below the cloud base and about 5 °C per kilometre above it. Temperature increases from left to right. At any altitude where the orange parcel line lies to the right of the violet environment line, the parcel is warmer than the surrounding air and keeps accelerating upward. Where the two lines cross, the parcel loses its buoyancy and stops.

blocks.caption: A summer day over farm country, with a warm layer a couple of kilometres up.
blocks.task: Grow a cumulus congestus: a tower several kilometres tall.

blocks.text: If there is no low-level inversion to cap a growing tower, it can climb to an altitude of 10 to 12 kilometres. Throughout the lowest layer of the atmosphere (the troposphere), the air generally gets colder with height because it is heated from below by the sun-warmed ground. Around 10 to 12 kilometres up, however, the temperature stops falling with altitude and begins to rise instead.

This upper warming is caused by **ozone**, a three-atom form of oxygen (O₃). High in the atmosphere, intense ultraviolet light from the sun splits ordinary two-atom oxygen molecules (O₂) apart, and the free oxygen atoms combine with intact oxygen molecules to form an ozone layer. Ozone strongly absorbs incoming ultraviolet radiation, heating the upper atmosphere from above while shielding the surface below.

The boundary where temperature stops falling and starts rising with height is the **tropopause**, marking the base of the **stratosphere**. Because the stratosphere gets warmer with altitude, it acts as a massive, permanent inversion lid across the top of the troposphere that even the strongest thunderstorm updraughts cannot penetrate far.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height, from the ground into the stratosphere.

blocks.text: When a rising storm tower slams into the stable tropopause, the buoyant air continuing to surge up from below cannot climb much higher and spreads out horizontally instead, like a fountain jet hitting a ceiling. At that altitude the cloud water is completely frozen, so the spreading ice crystals fan out into a broad, flat **anvil** with fibrous edges. Strong upper-level winds blow the anvil far downwind, usually stretching it out ahead of the storm’s path. Once a towering heap develops an icy upper region and begins dropping rain from its base, it has become a **cumulonimbus**, or thunderstorm.

In the next figure, you can also adjust how rapidly the surrounding atmosphere cools with height. Because a rising parcel inside the cloud cools at roughly 5 °C per kilometre, a steeper cooling rate in the surrounding air gives the cloudy parcel a larger temperature lead and stronger upward acceleration.

blocks.caption: The same day, with the instability control added.
blocks.task: Remove the lid and make the air unstable enough to grow a cumulonimbus.

blocks.text: An individual thunderstorm cell goes through a three-stage life cycle that lasts about an hour.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell, from first heap to last shower.
blocks.task: Run the storm to the end of its life.

blocks.text: In the **growing stage** (or cumulus stage), the tower consists entirely of warm updraughts carrying moist air skyward and building the cloud upward.

The **mature stage** begins when precipitation inside the cloud grows too heavy for the updraughts to support and starts falling toward the ground. Inside strong, gusty updraughts, ice pellets are repeatedly carried up and tumbled through dense clouds of supercooled droplets that freeze onto them in concentric layers, building **hailstones** until they are heavy enough to fall out of the storm.

As heavy rain and hail plunge downward, they drag surrounding air down with them. At the same time, drier air mixes into the edges of the storm and evaporates some of the falling rain, chilling the air and making it denser so it plunges faster still. During this mature stage, the storm contains a warm updraught and a cold downdraught side by side, producing its heaviest downpours, hail, lightning, and sudden surface wind gusts.

Finally, in the **dissipating stage**, the cold downdraught spreads out across the ground like a miniature cold front, cutting off the inflow of warm, humid air that fuelled the updraught. Starved of warm air from below, the storm rains itself out, often leaving its orphaned ice anvil lingering high overhead.

Radar shows the same life from outside. The first echo appears high in the growing tower, five or six kilometres up where ice and supercooled water meet, often ten to twenty minutes before any rain reaches the ground. In the mature stage the core reaches from the ground far up into the cloud, at 50 dBZ and more, and hail shows as a magenta heart in the middle of it. The anvil, made of small ice crystals, barely registers. At the end the echo sinks out of the bottom of the cloud as the last rain falls, and only the faint anvil is left.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell on radar at each stage of its life, sliced through the middle. The white shapes are the cloud; the colours are what the radar sees.

blocks.text: Inside a churning cumulonimbus tower, soft hailstones (graupel), ice crystals, and supercooled droplets constantly collide with one another. All atoms have negatively charged **electrons** on their outer shells, and when two objects rub or collide, electric charge can transfer from one surface to the other, just as rubbing a balloon on your hair leaves one negatively charged and the other positively charged.

In the mixed-phase zone of a thunderstorm, collisions between small ice crystals and heavier pellets of soft hail systematically leave the tiny ice crystals with a slight positive charge and the heavier hail pellets with a negative charge. The storm’s updraught sweeps the lightweight, positively charged ice crystals high into the anvil while gravity pulls the heavier, negatively charged hail into the middle and lower parts of the cloud, separating electrical charge on a massive scale.

blocks.caption: Where a thunderstorm keeps its charge.

blocks.text: Once the voltage difference between these regions (or between the cloud base and the ground) grows strong enough, the electric field strips electrons directly off air molecules, ionizing the air into an electrically conducting plasma channel. Stored charge surges through that narrow channel in a violent spark several kilometres long: **lightning**.

A lightning stroke heats the narrow channel of air to roughly 30,000 °C in a few millionths of a second—about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. Superheated that rapidly, the air has no time to expand gently; it explodes outward at supersonic speed, creating a shock wave that decays into the booming sound wave we hear as **thunder**.

Because light travels at 300,000 kilometres per second, you see the lightning flash the instant it happens. Sound travels through air much more slowly, at about **343 metres per second**, taking roughly **three seconds to travel one kilometre**. By counting the seconds between the flash and the first crack of thunder and dividing by three, you can find how many kilometres away the lightning struck. (The figure speeds up the clock so you don’t have to wait in real time, while displaying the actual number of seconds you would count.)

blocks.caption: A storm somewhere off over the hills.
blocks.task: Make the storm strike, and count.

blocks.text: Lightning does not only strike directly beneath the dark rain core. Because strong positive charge accumulates high up in the spreading anvil, a powerful lightning bolt can arc outward from the upper cloud through clear air and strike the ground ten kilometres or more away from the rain shaft, a hazard known as a "bolt from the blue."

The safety rule follows from this: if you count fewer than thirty seconds between flash and thunder, the storm is within ten kilometres and close enough to strike you. Get indoors straight away, away from open ground and ridges, and stay under cover until thirty minutes after the last rumble of thunder. A dying anvil can still fire a late bolt when the rain seems to be over.

A few distinctive cloud formations appear only when wind, moisture, and stability line up just right. You might go a whole summer without spotting one, and when you do, it goes in your journal as a rare entry.

When a strong, steady wind blows across a mountain ridge into a stable atmosphere, the air is forced up the windward slope, cools at 10 °C per kilometre, and becomes colder and denser than the surrounding air at the ridge crest. Gravity pulls that dense air back down the leeward side, where it picks up speed and overshoots its original starting altitude.

Because the surrounding air is stable (warming by less than 10 °C per kilometre going downward), the descending parcel—warming at the full 10 °C per kilometre—becomes warmer and more buoyant than its neighbours at the bottom of the dip and rebounds upward again. The airflow continues oscillating up and down for many kilometres downwind of the ridge in **standing mountain waves**, much like stationary ripples downstream of a boulder in a river. Wherever the wave crests lift a moist layer of air past its dew point, water vapour condenses into a stationary cloud right at the top of the wave.

blocks.caption: Wind blowing over a mountain ridge.
blocks.task: Get the wind and moisture right to make a lens cloud.

blocks.text: The resulting cloud is **altocumulus lenticularis** (from the Latin for lens-shaped), since the wave crests that condense moisture usually sit a few kilometres up on the middle floor. Unlike ordinary cellular altocumulus formed by radiative overturning, a lenticularis cloud is remarkably smooth and sculpted, often resembling an almond, a smooth lens, or a stack of plates hovering beside the peak even in a howling gale. Moist air continuously flows into the upwind edge, rises and cools below its dew point to form droplets, and then flows out the downwind edge, where it descends, warms back above its dew point, and evaporates. The cloud outline stays locked in place over the terrain while the wind races right through it.

Beneath the spreading anvil of a mature thunderstorm, the underside of the cloud sometimes develops smooth, rounded pouches hanging toward the ground. The anvil contains a heavy load of ice crystals and water droplets. When pockets of this particle-laden air sink into the drier air below the anvil base, the ice and droplets begin to evaporate (or sublimate), absorbing latent heat from the sinking parcel. Because that evaporation cools the air, the sinking parcel warms at only about 5 °C per kilometre as it descends, whereas the clear air surrounding it warms with decreasing altitude by 6 or 7 °C per kilometre. Staying colder and denser than the air around it, the cloudy pocket continues to sink in smooth, rounded lobes—essentially convection running upside down, driven by evaporation inside sinking air just as a cumulus tower is driven upward by condensation inside rising air.

blocks.caption: The underside of an anvil, late in a storm.
blocks.task: Let the cold air sink until pouches form.

blocks.text: These hanging pouches are called **mammatus** (or mamma). Although they look dramatic, especially when lit from the side by low evening sunlight, the pouches themselves are harmless descending air. Because they form underneath the spreading anvil, you will most often see them either well ahead of an approaching storm or trailing behind after the main storm core has passed.

An even rarer and more fleeting formation appears when strong vertical wind shear develops right across the top of a stable cloud layer, with a fast-moving current of air sliding directly over a slower, denser layer below. Just as wind blowing across a lake raises ripples on the water, the velocity difference across the boundary between the two air layers generates waves. As each wave crest pokes upward into the faster-moving upper stream, the fast wind pushes the top of the crest forward ahead of its slower-moving trough below. When the wind shear is strong enough to overcome the stability of the layer, the wave crests steepen and roll completely over into breaking curls.

blocks.caption: A cloud layer with fast air above and slower air below.
blocks.task: Increase the difference in wind until the waves curl over.

blocks.text: These breaking billows are **Kelvin-Helmholtz waves**, officially catalogued as *fluctus* in the International Cloud Atlas. Because the curling waves rapidly mix the two air layers together and erase the shear that created them, a train of *fluctus* billows usually lasts only a minute or two before dissipating. Spotting them takes good timing, and to aircraft pilots they are a clear visual warning of severe wind shear and turbulence.
First name each cloud in the photos, then read what a few changing skies are up to.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Cumulus heaps are already towering into congestus by midday on a hot, humid day. What should you expect by mid-afternoon?
items.why: Cumulus towers that are already growing tall by midday in a deeply unstable atmosphere often reach the tropopause by afternoon, developing into cumulonimbus thunderstorms with lightning, downpours, and gusty winds.

items.question: The morning balloon sounding shows a strong temperature inversion two kilometres up. What will today’s cumulus heaps do?
options: Flatten out beneath the lid in fair weather
items.why: When rising cumulus clouds hit a warmer inversion layer aloft, they become colder and denser than their surroundings and cannot climb through the cap.

items.question: You see a flash of lightning and hear thunder 12 seconds later. Roughly how far away was the strike?
items.why: Sound travels about one kilometre every three seconds, so 12 ÷ 3 gives 4 km—well within the 10 km danger zone where everyone should get indoors.

items.question: The rain has stopped and the last rumble of thunder was ten minutes ago. Is it safe to go back outside?
options: Not yet, wait until thirty minutes after the last thunder
Yes, as long as there is blue sky overhead
items.why: A dissipating storm anvil can still discharge lightning up to ten kilometres away through clear air; wait a full thirty minutes after the last thunder before going back out.

items.question: A smooth, lens-shaped cloud hovers motionless over the ridge all afternoon despite a strong wind aloft. What is it?
options: A lenticularis cloud in a standing mountain wave
Valley fog lifting up the slope
items.why: Strong wind blowing over a ridge into stable air sets up standing waves downwind; moisture condenses at the wave crest and evaporates on the leeward side, keeping the smooth lens stationary while the wind flows through it.

items.question: At dawn, miniature castle-like turrets sprout from a middle-level line of altocumulus. What should you expect?
options: Watch for thunderstorms developing this afternoon
items.why: Altocumulus castellanus shows that the middle floor is already unstable in the morning, meaning afternoon thermals will have no stable cap to stop them from growing into thunderstorms.

learned: A cumulus heap keeps growing as long as it remains warmer than the surrounding air; an inversion aloft can cap its growth, and forecasters classify heaps by vertical development as humilis, mediocris, or congestus.

The tropopause (10 to 12 km up) acts as a permanent inversion warmed by ozone in the stratosphere; a storm tower that reaches it spreads out into a flat ice anvil, forming a cumulonimbus thunderstorm.

A single thunderstorm cell lasts about an hour, progressing from an all-updraught growing stage, to a mature stage with both updraughts and precipitation-driven downdraughts, to a dissipating stage when the cold downdraught cuts off the warm inflow.

Because sound travels roughly one kilometre every three seconds, counting the seconds from lightning flash to thunder and dividing by three gives the strike distance in kilometres; if the count is under 30 seconds (within 10 km), get indoors and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

Rare cloud formations include stationary lenticularis lenses in standing mountain waves, hanging mammatus pouches cooled by evaporation beneath storm anvils, and breaking Kelvin-Helmholtz curls (fluctus) formed by strong wind shear.

cumulonimbus.title: Cumulonimbus
cumulonimbus.text: A towering convective cloud that climbs all the way to the tropopause (10 to 12 km up), where its frozen top flattens and spreads into a fibrous anvil. A single cell grows, matures, and dissipates in about an hour, capable of producing heavy downpours, hail, strong downdraught gusts, and lightning.

lightning.title: Counting the thunder
lightning.text: Collisions between soft hail and ice crystals inside a storm separate electric charge until a massive spark discharges as lightning, heating the air channel to about 30,000 °C and generating the shock wave we hear as thunder. Because sound travels about one kilometre every three seconds, dividing the seconds between flash and thunder by three gives the distance in kilometres. If the count is under 30 seconds (10 km), get indoors and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

lenticularis.title: Lens cloud (lenticularis)
lenticularis.text: A smooth, lens-shaped cloud hovering in the crest of a standing mountain wave downwind of a ridge. Moist air condenses as it rises into the wave crest and evaporates as it sinks out the downwind edge, keeping the cloud stationary in the sky while strong wind blows straight through it.

mammatus.title: Mammatus
mammatus.text: Smooth, rounded pouches hanging beneath a thunderstorm anvil, formed where pockets of ice- and droplet-laden air sink into drier air below. Evaporating particles chill the sinking parcels so they remain denser than their surroundings, driving upside-down convection. While they indicate a strong storm nearby, the pouches themselves are harmless.

fluctus.title: Kelvin-Helmholtz waves (fluctus)
fluctus.text: Lines of curling, breaking-surf billows along the top of a cloud layer, formed where a fast airstream slides over a slower, denser layer below. They last only a minute or two before mixing away and warn pilots of strong wind shear and turbulence.
